title: 'I turned down a much bigger contract so I could race where I wanted' – Paula Blasi officially signs for Movistar after drawn-out exit from UAE Team L'IMAD
author: James Moultrie
text:
Reigning Vuelta Femenina champion Paula Blasi has signed for Movistar for 2027, and the next three seasons, the Spanish Women's WorldTour team confirmed on Wednesday.

The 23-year-old announced back in September that she would be leaving UAE Team L'IMAD a year earlier than contracted, and that she had signed for a new team in 2027, but while it was widely reported that it would be Movistar, that wasn't confirmed until now.

The Spanish team have reportedly paid a hefty fee to buy her out of her contract with the Emirati squad, and secure her future.

Scorching a rapid path to becoming one of the best riders in the world, Blasi took massive victories at the Vuelta and Amstel Gold Race in just her first full season as a pro this year, also finishing fifth overall on debut at the Tour de France Femmes , and taking top-five finishes at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, La Flèche Wallonne, and the Tour Down Under.

"I'm at a point in my sporting career where I needed to take a different step and look for a team that believed in me, supported my goals and was as ambitious as I am," said Blasi.

"I'll be able to grow, share leadership responsibilities and learn from Marlen [Reusser], which will be important for my development as an athlete. And on top of that, it's my home team. It makes me even prouder to wear the jersey."

Blasi's exit from UAE Team L'IMAD has been a long and complex one, with plenty of speculation and drama surrounding the move which is one of the most significant transfers in the women's peloton this year.

According to Spanish newspaper , while Blasi is set to earn around €600,000 a year, she turned down significantly more money at UAE so that she could ride for Movistar, with an €85,000 buy-out clause reportedly being paid so she could exit early.

also explained why there was such a delay despite signing her new deal before the Worlds in September. This was due to the wait for approval from the UCI, after the Spanish team's boss Unzué and her agent Alex Carera – who also represents Tadej Pogačar – convinced her that the project at Movistar was the right one, having already started to look elsewhere.

"I turned down a much bigger contract so I could race where I wanted," Blasi told . "It’s no secret that UAE is one of the teams with the most money. If you turn it down, you’re surely turning down one of the biggest offers you could receive.

"I want to be in line with what’s going on and earn what I think I’m worth. But for me, it was more important to think about my sporting future. I didn’t want to earn a huge amount for three years and end up hanging up my bike because I couldn’t take it anymore. My priority was to go somewhere where I can sleep peacefully and my only goal is to train."

A homegrown star joins Movistar

Movistar described the arrival of Blasi as a further strengthening of the team's "commitment to women's cycling and to building a project capable of uniting the present and the future," adding her talent to the likes of established leaders Marlen Reusser and Liane Lippert, and rising young stars like Cat Ferguson, Paula Ostiz, and Alejandra Neira.

"We're extremely excited to finally announce Paula's arrival to our team for the next three seasons," said team boss Sebastián Unzué.

"Her signing represents another step forward in quality, allowing us to compete for the most important races on the calendar. I want to thank Paula for her trust and for believing in this project. We can't wait to start working together. Welcome, Paula!"

Blasi only turned professional in May 2025, making a mid-season jump from UAE's development team up to the WorldTour squad, where she impressed immediately, winning a stage and the best young rider classification at the WorldTour-level Tour de Romandie, and finishing sixth at the Tour de l'Avenir – but he improvement in 2026 has been nothing short of remarkable.

Her victory at the Vuelta – a historic first for Spain in the women's race, and marking the arrival of a new superstar – stemmed from two stunning second-place finishes to Les Praeres and the iconic Alto de l'Angliru, landing her the red jersey ahead of Anna van der Breggen.

The hype and transfer rumours followed Blasi everywhere for the rest of the season, with the confirmation having to wait until October that it was Movistar who had secured the most sure-fire prospect in the women's peloton, who looks set to lead the ongoing and next generation of stars.

title: Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
text:
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.

The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.

On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.

Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.

Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.

The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.

After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.

The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.

The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.

The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.

He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.

“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

title: EF Education-EasyPost pick up another climber for 2027 after Carapaz departure
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
Ivan Sosa will return to the WorldTour after two years away racing for the Kern Pharma team, as EF Education-EasyPost announced they have signed the Colombian for the 2027 season.

"I've heard great things about EF Education-EasyPost from riders on the team. They speak very highly of the team," Sosa said in the EF Education-EasyPost announcement.

"I think the team gave me the opportunity - and will continue to give me the opportunity - to come back and take that leap forward. And I believe that by working together with everyone who's part of the team, I know we're going to be able to achieve great things and we're going to have lots of happy moments - lots of victories that we'll experience along the way."

Sosa was one of several talented riders scouted from Colombia by former Androni Giocattoli manager Gianni Savio in 2017. After a successful two-year stint with the Italian outfit, Sosa signed with Ineos and spent three years with them before moving across to the Movistar Team. While Sosa has yet to win at the WorldTour level, he is a formidable climber and valuable domestique with victories in the Vuelta a Burgos and Tour de la Provence.

However, his results suffered as the years went on, but after undergoing iliac artery surgery in 2025, he found his way back to the top step of the podium in the Tour of Turkey, winning a stage and finishing second overall. Sosa then had a solid ride at the Vuelta a España, finishing in the top 10 on two stages after making the winning breakaway.

"Everything's just getting better and better. I'm growing more and more, and I feel better and better," Sosa said. "I'm really happy, really pleased, because I also had the chance to see how my body was holding up, and I realise that I'm fine now.

"It really motivates me to be able to rejoin the WorldTour and know that I'll have the team's support - everyone's support - and that we'll be able to improve and win races. That's what I want and what I think the team wants, too."

"Ivan is on his way to firing on all cylinders for the first time in a few years," Vaughters said. "He's going to be a huge help to our team when we're racing in the high mountains. He is savvy enough to get himself into a strong breakaway, and then he's strong enough to be able to make it to the finale.

"We saw him do that twice at the Vuelta a España. And after his recovery from iliac artery surgery, he has shown how motivated he is to race aggressively in search of wins. That's the kind of rider we look for."

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘We’re the worst team in the NBA’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
Isn’t it great to start the season with a loss in the standings…

…and a banner in the rafters?

Here’s what your Knickerbockers and Sixonians said after yesterday’s affair, one of 82 regular-season games. Breathe.

On the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony and the organization’s efforts to organize it:

“I would like to give, and I don’t know who was behind it, but you know, obviously starting with Mr. Dolan and everybody else, you know, did a fantastic job with the ceremony.

“So I would like to acknowledge, you know, everybody else who was behind it. You know, okay, like you said, everybody, you know, you guys did a fantastic job; they weren’t mud like us, so thank you.”

On the Knicks’ performance in their season-opening loss to the 76ers:

“You know, what an ugly game. I want to give the 76ers, Nick Nurse and his team, a lot of credit. A long night for them, but they came out and they tried to do what they needed to do to get a win, so you give them credit first of all. But there were some things that we could have done better. Our transition defense was not good with our starting group in the third quarter. All throughout the game we looked like we were running in mud. Whether it was in the front court or it was in transition, we were not good getting to our spots and putting pressure on Philadelphia the right way… We talked about taking care of the ball. We did a little bit better job. But in a one- or two-possession game when you have 15 turnovers for 22 points, it makes it tough.”

On the Knicks’ slow movement and poor offensive spacing:

“Part of us looking like we were running in mud was our spacing wasn’t great. We were walking everywhere, which hurt our spacing.”

On the Knicks’ transition defense and the 76ers’ fast-break scoring:

“They had nine fast-break points in the first half [in how the Knicks track it]. And then in the second half, they had 19 fast-break points. That’s where the game was won and lost, especially in the third quarter when our starters were out there.”

On how difficult the Knicks’ opening-night performance was to watch:

“I don’t know about you guys, but that was a tough one for me to watch.”

On why a late Jalen Brunson comeback would not have satisfied him even if the Knicks had won the game:

“If Jalen Brunson hits those shots down the stretch and we win, for me personally as their coach, there’s going to be something inside of me that wished it wouldn’t happen. It’s almost like you’re playing with fire and you ended up winning that time without any water or one of them fire blankets to cover the fire.”

On why the Knicks must improve their execution instead of relying on Brunson’s late-game heroics:

“Is (Brunson) capable of making those shots? Yes. But if we played the right way, then it wouldn’t come down to that. But we put ourselves in a hole not doing the little things. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t. And we have to watch the film and regroup and see how we can put a stretch of 48 minutes together.

“I want to win. Don’t get me wrong. Don’t get it twisted. I want to friggin’ win. But not at the expense of us skipping steps. So if he hits those shots down the stretch and we win, as a coach, there’s going to be something inside of me that wouldn’t be happy. Because it’s like you’re playing with fire, and you ended up winning that time without any water.”

On Andre Drummond’s debut:

“I thought that he played with a lot of bounce and energy. We probably ran him a little too long there because it looked like in the second half, not just him but all five of our starters too, ran a little bit out of gas.

“I have to keep getting to know him to see where the minutes may lie for him to be effective for us, but I thought that he was really really, really good on both ends of the floor during the first half.”

On the importance of the little things after the Knicks’ opening-night loss:

“We put ourselves in a hole not doing the other little things and, you know, sometimes it works at the end of the game, sometimes it doesn’t.”

On balancing the Knicks’ championship celebration with their opening-night responsibilities:

“It’s tough because, knock on wood, this could be a once in a lifetime thing. You never know. It’s hard. It’s hard to accomplish something like this.

“You definitely want guys to embrace it and celebrate it with each other because they went through a lot, with the fans, with the rest of the organization, and just with their families. So you don’t want to take that moment away from them. But in the same breath we obviously have a job to do tonight.”

On the Knicks’ slow start not defining their season:

“I keep telling myself that no matter what happens tonight — if we win by five, if we win by 20, if we lose by five, if we lose by 20 — there’s a lot of basketball left. Just because of whatever happens tonight is not going to define us. I would rather them enjoy the moment than me cutting it short or carving into their emotions based on their families and all that stuff being here. Like I said, it’s going to be hard to do, but that’s what we get paid to do so we’ll figure it out one way or another.”

On the atmosphere at Madison Square Garden and the uniqueness of Knicks fans:

“Opening nights are always exciting for everybody and anybody. It’s the start of something new for everybody. It’s fresh. Everybody is energized. You feel the buzz. I don’t care where you are, you feel a buzz. Obviously, here, with our fans, Knicks fans are just different. It’s as simple as that. They’re absolutely friggin’ different. And the buzz has been going on for a while. And you felt it today.

“I had a million texts coming. And usually during the course of the season, I have a couple texts coming before the game. But it was a boatload of them on the way. Couple of calls. … But you can feel it from the correspondence that get, which is different from a regular season game.”

On the Knicks raising a banner to commemorate their 2025 NBA Cup championship:

“I think it’s a recognition of what our journey was like last year. There were obviously a lot of ups and downs. Our guys rallied, found a way to win the NBA Cup and then (the) end-of-season final.”

On the Knicks needing to humble themselves after losing their season opener:

“I think it’s good for us to get knocked down off the mountain, humble ourselves, put our egos in check. I’ve told you guys since day one, whatever happens the first couple of weeks of the season, I’m not sure that’s who we really are.”

On the 76ers’ performance and his own shooting struggles:

“They’re really good and they made things difficult for us. Obvious for me, shots weren’t falling. We can make all the excuses in the world. Like I said, I’m just happy we can move forward now.”

On what failed for the Knicks in Tuesday’s loss:

“Transition defense, yeah. Our offense, I think we were good in spurts. But it’s not good enough.”

On the challenges of defending a championship after receiving so much praise:

“It’s going to be difficult. You have everyone praising us about what we’ve done a couple months ago. It’s just human nature.”

On thanking Knicks fans during the championship banner ceremony:

“Most importantly, I want to say thank you to you guys for not leaving Game 4. We really appreciate it. I mean, this is, as much as we won this, we wouldn’t have won this without you guys, I mean, this is unbelievable. This is really good. A dream come true.

“I know we’re all excited to get this season going. We’re ready to turn the page as a team. But one thing, I would like to say, the joy that this city had this summer we would love to replicate that again. Thank you, guys. Let’s raise this banner.”

On pursuing another NBA championship rather than defending last season’s title:

“Every year, it’s a new year to attack something. When people say we’re defending the title, I mean, that’s one way to look at it. But it’s something we won, we’ve put it in our past, and now we’re just trying to attack another.”

On the Knicks’ mentality after losing their season opener:

“We play basketball for a living. If you can’t get up and get excited to play basketball, no matter who the hell we play, you got to do some soul-searching. It doesn’t matter if we’re defending champs, it doesn’t matter if we have the worst record in the league last year. No matter what we got to make sure we are professionals and do what our job is and at the end of the day, I don’t think anybody picked us to win the championship again.

“So nothing to it. We shouldn’t sit there and think we’re the champions because we’re not. We’re 0-1. We’re the worst team in the NBA as of right now. So we need to play like it.”

On the improved Eastern Conference and the Knicks’ need to dictate how they play:

“Obviously, they played well, and the East got shaken up a little bit. We have to make sure we’re prepared for what every team is going to try and do, and what we want to do. We can’t let them dictate what we want to do. For us, nothing changes. It’s the same ol’ process. We have to make sure we perfect it the best we can.”

On the Knicks failing to match the level of play of last season’s team:

“I just thought that we put ourselves too much in a deficit, and you know we’re not that Knick team yet from last year.”

“To celebrate one last time with the fans, it means a lot. We wanted to give them a better version of ourselves tonight than we did, but it was really special to have that moment here again in New York after 53 years.”

On the Knicks receiving favorable officiating on Tuesday after winning the championship:

“They getting that championship whistle. They win one chip, they get a championship whistle.”

On the 76ers’ defensive rebounding adjustments against the Knicks:

title: Goodbye, Quick-Step: 24 Years of Cobbles, Glory, and Swagger
author: ahood
text:
Boonen was the face of much of the Quick-Step classics heyday. (Photo: Equipe Ploeg /(c)Tim De Waele/Getty Images)

Quick-Step will close a 24-season run as title sponsor that helped turn a Belgian flooring brand into something synonymous with winning bike races.

Before today’s “superteam” era, Quick-Step was the powerhouse that drove the elite men’s peloton.

OK, other teams were obsessing on the Tour de France , but Quick-Step was the team for everything else.

For Belgians, it was their New York Yankees.

Museeuw, Boonen , Gilbert, Evenepoel — it was the team where all the big Belgian stars ended up. And few other superstars along the way as well.

Quick-Step remains a partner through 2030, but one of cycling’s longest title name partnerships is ending.

Starting in 2003, Patrick Lefevere built the squad into the “Wolfpack,” a winning machine that won across multiple terrain. Sprints, escapes, stage wins were all part of the team ethos.

But it was the classics that were essential to the team’s DNA.

The Quick-Step relationship began with Mapei in 1999, then Lefevere launched Quick-Step-Davitamon in 2003. Tom Boonen became a Belgian superstar and carried team colors for a decade.

By the 2020s, Quick-Step — a multinational flooring company — was struggling to keep pace with deep-pocketed superteams that now dominate the men’s peloton.

Czech billionaire Zdeněk Bakala remains behind the scenes, and Jurgen Foré took over as general manager after Lefevere retired.

Safety Jogger takes Quick-Step’s place alongside Soudal on the team kit in 2027. And with longtime bike sponsor Specialized also leaving, it’s an end of an era .

Even with Remco Evenepoel gone, the team is still finding ways to win. Tim Merlier and Paul Magnier now carry its winning legacy.

Here are nine chapters that explain why Quick-Step’s place in cycling history will be hard to replace.

Quick-Step’s roots run through Mapei. The powerhouse of the 1990s won world titles and sprints, and its classics roster ran so deep that Lefevere could call in the winning order at Paris-Roubaix.

By 2003, Mapei was gone, and Lefevere built Quick-Step-Davitamon with riders and staff from Mapei and Domo-Farm Frites.

The Belgian super-squad immediately delivered, with Museeuw winning Het Volk and Bettini taking Milan-San Remo in its debut season.

Only Lotto — which started in 1985 — and Cofidis and FDJ — both in 1997 — have sponsored an elite men’s pro team longer.

Quick-Step soon were the bulldogs of the spring classics. The team expected to win and became so good that even podiums were viewed as disappointments.

Bettini gave the team a champion who could win beyond the pavé . Racing for Italy, he took Olympic road gold in Athens in 2004, then consecutive world titles in 2006 and 2007.

Lefevere squeezed the value out of those victories, and Bettini emerged as the Italian swashbuckler who helped define the team’s early years.

Back in trade-team colors, the Cricket won consecutive editions of Lombardia in 2005 and 2006.

It’s hard to describe how big Tom Boonen was at the peak of his powers.

Boonen came along as Museeuw was fading and Belgian fans were hungry for a young, brash winner. They found one in Boonen, who soon became “Tomeke.”

After Lefevere stole him from Johan Bruyneel and U.S. Postal Service, Boonen lifted the team to new heights.

His career took off with huge wins at the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix in 2005. The world title in Madrid that fall made Boonen the perfect star for a new century of bike racing.

Boonen brought some football swagger to cycling, along with some off-the-bike drama, and his rivalry with Fabian Cancellara on the cobbles dominated the classics. His every move was front-page news in Belgium.

Quick-Step had its defining rider, and Belgium had its new two-wheeled idol. Lefevere loved it.

Lefevere never had the rider to chase yellow, but he built one of cycling’s best cobblestone teams.

At its peak, the crew was more than just Boonen. Stijn Devolder won Flanders in both 2008 and 2009, and Niki Terpstra was showing signs of future success.

Then came Boonen’s extraordinary 2012 season, with victories at E3 Harelbeke, Gent-Wevelgem, Flanders, and Roubaix. His long solo into the Roubaix velodrome sealed a record-tying fourth victory and the finest classics campaign of his career.

His chance to make Roubaix history with a fifth cobble was stymied by Mat Hayman in 2016, the last of his epic cobblestone dramas.

Boonen’s retirement in 2017 could have left a hole no signing could fill.

Philippe Gilbert helped people get over it. His audacious solo victory at the 2017 Tour of Flanders and hard-earned 2019 Paris-Roubaix triumph extended the team’s northern reign. Terpstra added the 2018 Flanders title between them.

Dubbed the “Wolfpack,” this was Lefevere’s dream machine, capable of winning multiple monuments with a fleet of classics crushers.

Quick-Step leaves with the team’s impressive monument legacy with 24 monuments from 2003 to 2026. They won them all during that run multiple times.

Alaphilippe won Strade Bianche, Milan-San Remo, and La Flèche Wallonne in 2019 before turning the Tour upside down.

No one ever thought Alaphilippe could win the Tour until that magical 2019 edition. Two stage victories, 14 days in yellow, and fifth overall made him the race’s great disruptors.

Lefevere never got a Tour winner, but Alaphilippe made everyone believe, at least going deep into week 3.

Consecutive world road titles in 2020 and 2021 confirmed that Alaphilippe was more than some d’Artagnan on wheels.

Lefevere had an eye for talent and wasn’t afraid to take chances on people. Gilbert was the perfect example.

Some thought his best days were behind him, but with Lefevere, Gilbert won a pair of dream races.

The same thing happened with Mark Cavendish. The slowing Manxman was still hanging around, but Lefevere offered a lifeline when his career appeared close to over.…

title: Severely ill ICE detainees face imminent deportation to unknown African states, advocates say
author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
text:
Flights to third countries where the detainees have no ties are scheduled as early as Wednesday, relatives detail

Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms

Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.

Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.

The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions had been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.

“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa ,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.

“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”

The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.

Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband had been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “ Alligator Alcatraz ” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.

“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.

“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa.’

“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway.’ We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”

Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.

“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.

Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.

“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”

Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.

Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.

“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”

During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.

Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.

Advocates say Donald Trump ’s sweeping second-term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that the DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.

The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.

A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

title: 'Performances aren’t what you’d expect from a cyclist of his calibre' – Mystery surrounds Juan Ayuso’s 2026 race form
author: Owen Rogers
text:
After an excellent start to his time with Lidl-Trek, Juan Ayuso ’s 2026 season didn’t go so well, with the 24-year-old failing to meet expectations; now his team are examining the rider’s data to ensure he is in top form for 2027.

After four years with UAE Team Emirates-XRG, Ayuso’s move to Lidl-Trek was one of the headlines of last year’s transfer season, and he was expected to challenge for the podium in Grand Tours. Though his overall victory at the Volta ao Algarve in February was a good start, his season has tailed off somewhat, with diminishing results.

Hopes were high when he took third overall at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (formerly Critérium du Daupiné) after finishing second on the two mountain stages, but seventh place at the Tour de France, behind his former UAE teammate, Tadej Pogačar, was a disappointment.

His lacklustre season has caused some head-scratching at Lidl-Trek, where they have been unable to pinpoint why Ayuso is unable to deliver the results they had expected.

"Something’s wrong, that’s clear; something’s not right, because what we’re seeing isn’t normal. The verifiable data we have from training doesn’t add up. The sessions have gone well; Juan has sacrificed a lot and invested a great deal to be in top form, with seasons at altitude and specific preparation for the World Championships, but then the race comes and things don’t go his way. His performances aren’t what you’d expect from a cyclist of his calibre.

"He’s sad, of course. He’s an ambitious and very hardworking guy. When we talk after the races, he asks me, 'Aritz, what do you think? What do you think is going on?’ And I tell him, 'I don’t know, Juan, we don’t have the answer.'"

"Right now, we’re in the analysis phase, trying to pinpoint the problem to understand what’s happening. And in that process, we’re looking at everything, from his health, with any potential medical issues, to his training data."

While Ayuso has been struggling, his team have been busy in the market, signing a raft of talent, including GC podium finisher Felix Gall , who joins from Decathlon-CMA CGM after a season where he finished second at the Giro d’Italia and third in the Vuelta a España.

Despite the Austrian’s arrival, there should be no change to what is expected from Ayuso.

"Juan’s goals for 2027 have to be the same as in 2026: to compete in a Grand Tour, one-day classics, and week-long races, which is what he’s done in his final years as a professional," Arberas continued.

"He’s a top rider, one of those from whom victories are expected, and he knows it; he’s fully aware of it."

Despite his experience and a palmarès which already includes 18 victories, Ayuso is still only 24 and, theoretically at least, he has plenty of time to mature into the Grand Tour challenger he was expected to. But with the constant influx of hungry, young talent into the sport, the pressure must surely be on.

title: Florian Lipowitz contemplates change of approach heading into second season as Red Bull leader alongside Remco Evenepoel
author: James Moultrie
text:
German stage-racing specialist Florian Lipowitz is eyeing a change in approach for the upcoming 2027 season, looking to improve his overall offering as a rider with more one-day Classics on his calendar.

Speaking on , Lipowitz already floated the idea and said: "I simply need to focus a bit more on one-day races and improve there," which Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk has backed, saying it could help with his talents as a GC racer.

"I would even welcome that, because one-day races are ridden even harder than stage races," said Denk as reported by .

But he also asserted that "it has to be the right fit," for Lipowitz, one of the German squad's key leaders. "It's a balancing act."

A former Tour de France podium finisher in just his third year as a professional, Lipowitz entered 2026 with a schedule of only one-week stage races and the Tour de France – except for a team time trial dress rehearsal at the Trofeo Ses Salines – until he got injured.

While his level constantly improved from eighth in the Algarve to third in Catalunya, second in the Basque Country and Romandie, and finally to victory at the Tour of Slovenia, Lipowitz had his Tour abruptly ended during the stage 16 time trial. In one of the tightest corners, he crashed hard and broke his collarbone , abandoning the race having been sat fifth overall and in the race for the podium.

"I felt incredibly sorry for him at the time," said Denk, detailing how he then reassured Lipowitz, who started as co-leader alongside Remco Evenepoel at the Tour.

"We made it clear to him that he was on par with the very best in the first half of the season. He achieved podium finishes in Catalonia, the Basque Country, and Romandie. In addition, he won the Tour of Slovenia."

Lipowitz eventually made his return to racing at the Giro della Toscana, 50 days after his crash, and ended his season with four one-day race appearances, including at the World Championships in Montreal, finishing 47th.

Denk is eyeing up the brutally difficult Worlds road race in Haute-Savoie next year for Lipowitz, another reason for wanting to add more Classics to his calendar in preparation.

"The World Championships are incredibly tough with 5,000 metres of elevation gain, and that's exactly what Florian is suited to," said the team boss. "Therefore, it would be good if he did one or two one-day races beforehand."

He was due to race another one-day race in support of Evenepoel at Il Lombardia, but was forced to miss out due to illness.

Denk is certain the 26-year-old would have played a "good role" there, and said: "We missed him there – due to illness. I would have liked to have him with us." Evenepoel rode to fourth as Paul Seixas took solo victory.

Lipowitz and Evenepoel did butt heads momentarily during their Tour together as co-leaders, after the Belgian called out his teammate for not giving him a lead-out on stage 6, but the team and both riders squashed any potential issues the next morning. While their cooperation as co-leaders didn't get to play out fully after the German crashed out, Evenepoel's improvement in level to take second overall behind Pogačar adds to his standing as the team's main leader.

No decisions have been made yet over who will get leadership at which Grand Tour in 2027; they will only be confirmed on December 11 at the team's media day, but it would be unlikely to see Evenepoel not race the Tour again – even if he has said the door is not closed to potentially returning to the Giro d'Italia.

For Lipowitz, whose status is advanced as the German team's top home rider – an important figure for their German and Austrian title sponsors – his 2025 third place finish still holds him in good stead to potentially go back to the Tour, but Denk and his sporting management staff may want to spread their GC stars out, especially with Primož Roglič leaving the team.

When asked who would be riding where early into the off-season, Denk said: "That's a question that can be discussed. The outcome is still open," with the Tour route to be revealed on Thursday, October 22, and the Giro and Vuelta route to come out in November and December.

In 2026, Red Bull finished on the podium of all three Grand Tours: third at the Giro with Hindley, second at the Tour with Evenepoel, and second at the Vuelta with Roglič.

Denk's highlighted how "we've already won the Giro and know what that feels like. It definitely has its charm," suggesting he could be eyeing up sending one of his two main leaders to the Italian Grand Tour, though that spot could go to one of Hindley, or Italian riders Giulio Pellizzari and Lorenzo Finn, with Denk opting for Evenepoel and Lipowitz together at the Tour again.

title: F1 races to return to standard distance in 2028
text:
Formula 1 grands prix will return to their standard distance in 2028 after the maximum length was shortened for next season.

The maximum distance of a race was cut by 15km from 305km (189.5 miles) to 290km (180.2 miles) for the 2027 season.

That reduction was introduced because of a quirk of the situation surrounding changes to the engine rules for next year.

The new hybrid engines introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have been criticised for reducing the impact of driver skill.

The power split will be changed, in two steps, to 60-40 by 2028, enabling drivers to have maximum power for longer.

This means the cars will use more fuel - and that became a concern when it emerged some teams wanted to carry their chassis over into next year to save money.

As the fuel tank is within the chassis and therefore its size could not be changed, this meant those teams might not have been able to finish grands prix with their existing fuel tanks.

The change affects only a handful of races where fuel consumption is heaviest.

The sport's governing body, the FIA, published the 2027 rules this week and these included a section on changes for 2028 in which there is a clause that removes the reduction and reinstates the 305km maximum distance.

Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton had previously objected to the shortening of race distances.

Britain's Hamilton, 41, said: "The races should be longer because the races are physically easier than ever before. So shortening, I don't think, makes much sense.

"This is supposed to be the sport that's the most physically demanding - mentally and physically. There are some that are just so hot and ultimately you are on the edge. Like Singapore is incredibly hot and demanding.

"But that's where I think you want to see athletes - just right on the edge, right? Right at the edge of their performance, having to actually push their bodies further because that's what this sport is about - pushing, pushing the levels and pushing the boundaries."

title: 'It's a team I've always wanted to be part of' – Michael Valgren makes Netcompany Ineos switch for 2027
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Netcompany Ineos have announced the latest addition to their squad for the 2027 season, with Danish racer Michael Valgren joining on a two-year deal.

He joins after spending six years with EF Education-EasyPost and becomes Netcompany Ineos ' ninth addition of the off-season.

"To finally have the opportunity to join Netcompany Ineos is a dream come true. It's a team I've always wanted to be part of, so in many ways, it feels like things have come full circle," Valgren said.

"I'm really looking forward to joining such a special organisation, where no stone is left unturned in the pursuit of performance. I believe the environment and resources here can help me find those extra few percent to raise my level and continue fighting for victories.

"Just as importantly, I want to use my experience to help bring the group together, support our collective efforts in races and guide the talented young riders coming through the team. That's something I'm really motivated by.

"I'm also really looking forward to working with Geraint Thomas, someone I've admired throughout my career. His dedication and work ethic have always been a source of inspiration for me, and I hope I can play my part in carrying on the legacy he's built within the team."

Valgren has been a solid Classics rider during his time in the professional peloton with Tinkoff-Saxo, Astana, Dimension Data, and EF. Alongside his two big WorldTour Classics victories are wins at the Coppa Sabatini and Giro della Toscana, as well as further podiums at Amstel, the Bretagne Classic, and at the 2021 Road World Championships in Leuven.

In recent years, Valgren has battled back from a career-threatening crash suffered in June 2022, which left him with a fractured pelvis, ruptured ACL, MCL and meniscus in his knee.

He returned to action the following April, under contract with EF's development team, before moving back up to the WorldTour squad in 2024. This season has represented a comeback of sorts to his previous top level, having scored a stage 5 breakaway victory at Tirreno-Adriatico in addition to that Giro stage win.

"I've known Michael personally for a long time, and I've always had a lot of respect for him, both as a rider and as a person. He's a great character who I know will fit really well into the team," said Netcompany Ineos director of racing, Geraint Thomas.

"He brings a huge amount of experience and has shown he's still racing at an incredibly high level, particularly after everything he's been through following his crash. To come back from that and be winning big races again says a lot about his character and determination.

"He'll bring real strength and experience to our Classics group, but just as importantly, he'll be a great addition to the team off the bike too. We're really looking forward to having him with us."

Valgren is the latest rider to join Netcompany Ineos as the squad gets overhauled for 2027. He joins James Shaw and Markel Beloki in switching over from EF, while other notable names to join the British team include Clément Champoussin, Harold Tejada (both from XDS-Astana), and highly-rated Spanish junior double world champion Benjamin Noval .

The Tour de France returns to Britain in 2027 for the first time since 2014, with both the men’s and the women’s Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift getting underway in the country, and the men’s team presentation will take place on Wednesday, June 30, two days before racing gets underway.

The event will take place in the grounds of Edinburgh Castle and will be presented by the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, celebrating Scottish culture as well as showcasing the riders on stage in front of the public.

On a hill above the city, the location has limited access and ticketing is necessary, but the cost, starting at £27 (€32, US$36) per ticket, is not cheap, especially for a race which is otherwise free to attend.

While some Tour de France team presentations have been ticketed, especially when held in a location with limited capacity, they are generally free of charge. The most recent example of fans having to pay to witness the event was in 2014, when the race last started in Britain. Then, access to the First Direct Arena in Leeds cost upwards of £45.

"Featuring Highland dancers, massed pipes and drums, and new music created specially for the occasion, the ceremony will celebrate Scotland's culture and creativity while marking the start of an historic Grand Départ," the organisers' press release stated.

"While the opening ceremony and presentation of the riders take place on the Esplanade of Edinburgh Castle, the celebrations will extend beyond its walls, giving fans across Scotland’s capital the chance to see the riders en route to the Castle and join in the festivities ahead of the Grand Départ,

If you’ve signed up for the Grand Départ GB newsletter, you will have early access to tickets starting from midday on Friday, October 23, with members of British Cycling, Scottish Cycling and Beicio Cymru able to buy them 24 hours later.

If you’re a Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo customer you can purchase your tickets from midday on Monday, October 26, with general public sales beginning at the same time on Friday, October 30. Full details can be found here .

The race begins in Edinburgh on Friday, July 2, heading into England to finish in Carlisle. Stage 2 takes the riders from Keswick to Liverpool, with the third stage entirely in Wales, starting in Welshpool and finishing in Cardiff.

There will be a separate presentation event ahead of the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, though details will be announced in the coming months.

title: Tofik Beshir out of ICU and responsive after severe training crash
author: Matilda Price
text:
Beshir, 19, was training near his Lees-McRae College in North Carolina when the incident happened, and he was airlifted to hospital in Tennessee where he remained unconscious and in ICU with "injuries consistent with brain shear trauma".

He was later moved to a hospital in Washington D.C. to receive ongoing care.

His team and family have decided not to share many specific medical details about the extent of Beshir's injuries, but in the latest update, Hall confirmed that he has left the ICU.

"In the past few days, Tofik has been moved out of the ICU and he is responsive," he said. "This is incredible news for him and his progress, but he still has a long way to go."

"Your thoughts and your prayers, they're working, they are absolutely working, so please keep sending those his way, to his family and to our team," Hall said. "He has a long way to go, and we are still in need of that miracle. We believe more good things are coming, but he needs everyone to continue praying and thinking about him."

Born in Virginia to Ethiopian parents, Beshir is a freshman at Lees-McRae college and has been racing on the US cyclo-cross circuit since he was a junior.

He took his first elite victory last winter, and this year raced the USCX series with the CXD Trek Bikes team. He won five of the six races to secure the overall series title just a few days before his crash.

title: Cycling airbag system Aerobag named one of the best inventions of 2026
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
A new wearable airbag safety device for cyclists has made it onto magazine's list of best inventions in 2026.

Belgian company Aerobag's device is among 15 entries in the magazine's list under the 'sports & fitness' category, among a total of 300 inventions "making the world better, smarter, and more fun" this year, Time say.

Aerobag is a system fitted into the straps of bib shorts which, according to the company, "uses nine sensors scanning 200 times per second to monitor body dynamics and detect crash anomalies". The airbag "deploys in 100 milliseconds" when it's triggered before folding back into place, allowing the rider to continue racing afterwards.

The Aerobag team, headed by Bert Celis, spent six years developing the Aerobag. They began work on the device after Bjorg Lambrecht's death at the 2019 Tour de Pologne.

"You're sending athletes down the road at 60, 70, 90k an hour in lycra. And that was it. That was the catalyst. My mission, my absolute mission, is that you, as a rider, wake up at home. You don't wake up in the back of an ambulance."

It remains to be seen whether wearable airbags such as Aerobag will make it to professional cycling.

The brand is are already working with several kit manufacturers including Nalini, Nimbl, and MOA, with Picnic PostNL and Visma-Lease a Bike having already tested the device.

Meanwhile, back in February, the UCI launched a consultation on the use of wearable safety technology. The governing body invited 'expressions of interest' from relevant parties to form working groups.

"Already in contact with several players in the sector, the UCI now wishes to broaden the initiative to the greatest number possible of manufacturers and institutes working on the development of airbags and technical apparel for cyclists," the UCI stated at the time.

"The objectives of this initiative are as follows... Regarding airbag systems: to define a clear framework and appropriate standards to enable the development and integration of such devices into cycling (in competition and training); Regarding technical apparel: to study the integration of airbag solutions into clothing and to identify ways to further strengthen the protection offered by textiles."

title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
text:
The Chancellor was on a early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.

From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.

The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.

The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.

Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.

These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.

On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.

While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.

The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.

The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.

The latest inflation figure also applies as the uprating to tens of billions in welfare payments next April.

By law, benefits such as personal independence payment (PIP) and carer's allowance must rise in line with September's consumer price index (CPI) measure of inflation.

The figure also confirms that the Triple Lock will see the State Pension increase by 3.9% next April.

There is one form of relief here - food price inflation remains largely unaffected by the energy shock.

While higher inflation at a time of frozen tax thresholds will raise more tax in cash terms, it will also increase the cost of public services, including likely union pay demands.

All the while, UK borrowing costs have risen alongside most of the advanced world as the US-Israel war against Iran has intensified.

The Jackdaw gas field decision is seen as the start of a run of "pro growth" pre-Budget announcements.

It sends a directional message, but will not fundamentally change the trade off between cost of living breathing space, and delivering a Budget that convinces the markets and investors.

The fact the borrowing costs gap has narrowed a bit with other G7 nations, and the IMF praised pencilled-in plans to shrink borrowing, provided a platform for the chancellor's Budget.

The latest economic numbers amply illustrate the challenge of actually delivering them.

title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
text:
The pace of UK price rises accelerated ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The rate of inflation rose to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continued to squeeze global oil supplies.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

The wars in the middle east and Ukraine have pushed up fuel prices. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."

He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field .

The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".

The figures came as the ONS said the government borrowed £25bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.

title: Richard Carapaz departure was 'the simple option' to cut costs, says EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Carapaz has been the US team’s star rider over the past four seasons, finishing on the Giro d’Italia podium in 2025 and also in the top 10 of the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, while winning nine races including three Tour stages.

This year’s Tour was a standout, as he won two mountain stages and clinched the polka-dot jersey the team have coveted for so long, and he capped off his season with fourth place at the Vuelta.

However, despite that success and despite having another year left on his contract, Carapaz will move on in 2027, which is explained primarily by the team's ailing finances.

"It was a little bit of a sad situation where our economic resources were stretched to the point that we needed to make some hard decisions," Vaughters told .

Vaughters indicated that the team were facing budget cuts of around 15%, with the departure of Oatly – a title sponsor of the women’s WorldTour squad – a key reason, alongside soaring operational costs.

"When it comes down to like, 'Well, what are the cost centres that you can get rid of?' Well, there's not so many options, right? A very simple option would be to just let your most highly compensated rider leave."

As such, it would appear that Carapaz was not exactly poached by NSN Cycling.

"We willingly let Richie go. It was not forced," Vaughters said.

EF Education-EasyPost have been active in the transfer window but have focused on value for money, picking up the struggling former Giro d’Italia winner Tao Geoghegan Hart on a one-year deal, as well as the former junior world champion Emil Herzog.

title: Parents and teachers in England: share your views on two-week half terms
author: Guardian community team
text:
We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms

While it used to be standard for state schools in England to have one-week half terms, some pupils and staff are being given a fortnight off.

Councils set the holiday dates for state schools in England, while academies, free schools, foundation schools and voluntary-aided schools can set their own. Most schools still opt for one week, but more around the country are moving to, or considering the move to, a two-week break.

In the past, parents with young children have the said the longer holiday places an extra burden on them to find childcare . In Wales, plans to extend the half-term and reduce the summer term were shelved in 2024 after opposition from the teaching unions.

We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms. Do you think they are a good idea or not? Do you have a fortnight off? Do you have any concerns?

title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
author: Associated Press
text:
Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.

The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.

The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.

Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.

“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.

Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.

“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.

Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.

The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.
